documents.title: Medical Professionalism in the New Millennium Physician Charter

chunks.content: Background Ethical discussions of allocating lifesaving treatments in cases of emergencies are not new. Many vignettes have been previously articulated, referring, for example, to ICU beds, dialysis machines, etc [ – ]. The Covid-19 pandemic, however, presented an unprecedented scenario in constraining the allocation of scarce lifesaving medical resources. Medical teams worldwide faced an emergency situation characterized by mass morbidity and mortality, as well as great uncertainty that required, in real time, a swift decision to allocate respirators [ , ] and later, extra-corporal-oxygenation (ECMO) devices when demand for them highly exceeded the supply [ ]. This extreme scenario of shortages of lifesaving treatments generated uncertainty and required an accounting of complex ethical considerations to support fair and efficient allocation [ ]. Given the inherently relative and subjective nature of ‘fairness,’ the decision-making processes were often fragmented and lacked uniformity. As pandemic intensified, medical teams rushed to the front lines and, facing an unprecedented number of patients, became the most significant group in determining allocation of scarce lifesaving medical resources. In fact, a range of prioritization mechanisms was invoked in different sites [ , ]. Several studies reported that medical teams at early stages of the pandemia felt unprepared to face the ethical questions of allocating lifesaving resources [ ], giving high-volume assistance informed by medico-legal helplines [ ], and coping with uncertainty that eventually harmed their psychological status and wellbeing 11]. Ultimately, guidelines for scarce resource allocation should rest on a foundation of medical professionalism [ , ] that reflects a commitment both to patients’ autonomy and to social justice based on cost-effective management of limited clinical resources [ , ]. The definition of a balanced medical professionalism, however, may vary in accordance with cultural characteristics [ ] and different healthcare systems may apply a variety of perspectives toward prioritization, secondary to professional ethics, social values, clinical guidelines, available resources, and more [ , , ]. Various prioritization strategies for fairness in allocation have been developed over the years [ ]. Different ethical principles reflect distinct aspects of justice and equity that may clash with each other. For example, the egalitarianism approach prescribes equal treatment of all patients and suggests that patients should be prioritized on the basis of ‘first-come– first-served’ or by random draw (lottery) [ , ]. In contrast, the value of utilitarianism highlights the need to prefer individuals who have the best chance of survival, based on the rationale of saving as many lives as possible [ , ]. This perspective may set patients’ age as a threshold for receiving treatment [ , ]. Cultural Dimensions of an Ethical Challenge Despite the body of knowledge that has been amassed over the decades, the Covid-19 pandemic presented an extreme scenario of shortage of lifesaving treatments that generated uncertainty and required an accounting of complex ethical considerations that might assure fair and efficient allocation [ ]. Given the inherently relative and subjective nature of ‘fairness,’ the decision-making processes were often fragmented and lacked uniformity. As this excruciatingly challenging situation was being dealt with, several scholars suggested that healthcare workers may also be influenced by their cultural background, affecting their practice predispositions and perceptions of treatment recommendation [ , ]. Culture significantly influences ethical decision-making, particularly through implicit biases affecting interactions between healthcare providers and patients. Although these biases operate unconsciously, numerous studies have demonstrated that providers’ implicit biases (e.g., pro-White bias) can directly contribute to healthcare disparities via clinical decision-making, and indirectly through clinical interactions, communication patterns, and patients’ perceptions of care [ , ]. Another dimension of cultural impact involves peer relationships within healthcare teams required to collaboratively make critical decisions, frequently under high-pressure emergency conditions such as those encountered during the COVID-19 pandemic. To better understand cultural differences in these circumstances, it is worth considering critical consciousness , which denotes the anchoring of a reflective self with others into social interactions with patients and peers [ , ]. Critical consciousness includes awareness of elements, power relations, and conditions of injustice that are embedded in social relationships including healthcare. Beyond the concept itself, critical consciousness is oriented to pragmatic actions that should be considered in real-life experience [ ]. Despite the recognized importance of culture in shaping clinical practices particularly within multicultural contexts, to the best of our knowledge, little is known about cultural-based preferences among medical professionals regarding allocation of scarce resources, particularly during the Covid-19 pandemic. Thus, in this study we emphasize the relevance of medical professionals’ cultural characterizations and its potential influence on their preferences regarding the allocation of ECMO machines- an extreme situation of tiebreaker decisions concerning two or more eligible patients ‘competing’ for available crucial care [ , ]. This study was conducted in Israel – a multicultural society in which Arab and Jewish healthcare professionals treat Arab and Jewish patients equally.

Thus, in this study we emphasize the relevance of medical professionals’ cultural characterizations and its potential influence on their preferences regarding the allocation of ECMO machines- an extreme situation of tiebreaker decisions concerning two or more eligible patients ‘competing’ for available crucial care [ , ]. This study was conducted in Israel – a multicultural society in which Arab and Jewish healthcare professionals treat Arab and Jewish patients equally. Currently, the Arab population in Israel accounts for 21% of the general population whereas 45% of new M.D. licenses in 2021 were issued to Arabs. Nonetheless, healthcare disparities and inequalities between the Arab and Jewish communities have been documented in relation of chronic disease rates, access to healthcare facilities, and access to diagnostic tests [ – ]. In this study, we examined healthcare professionals’ perspectives toward equity in light of these facts. Our aim was to examine, in a real-time situation, the ethical perceptions of healthcare professionals with different cultural backgrounds- Jewish and Arab, in relation of the allocation of scarce medical resources (ECMO devices). These circumstances provided a unique opportunity to capture and analyze a snapshot of a significant event that tested collaborative, multicultural ethical decision-making process. We reached nurses and physicians during the final training of their academic managerial program, emerging as potential clinical leaders. In particular, our aim was twofold: (1) to conduct an exploratory study examining the perspectives of future managers and (2) to employ an interpretative approach to better understand whether the decision-making process is more influenced by a commitment to professionalism or by cultural factors. We hypothesized that we would find differences in perceptions between Jewish and Arab therapists, in light of their experience as professionals and citizens, complementary to the possibility of an influence of cultural perception on individual doctors’ ethical perspectives. Finally, we discuss adopting and implementing critical consciousness as a supportive framework to address ethical discrepancies in complex decision-making tasks within multicultural healthcare teams. Method Sample Following institutional ethics committee approval (No. 0008-22-ASF) a nationwide survey was conducted among healthcare workers (nurses and physicians) during the final stages of their academic managerial training. We approached three large academic centers in Israel offering advanced managerial programs in healthcare, reflecting multi-regional stratification and cross-national representation. All trainees in their final semester were directly invited to participate in the study. The selection of a population of future medical managers reflects a purposive sampling approach, intentionally focusing on a relatively homogeneous group of professionals attended to play a critical role in policy-making in future, including emergency scenarios. Thus, addressing similar ethical dilemmas in real time. Accordingly, the essential training during COVID 19 pandemic included explanations regarding ECMO machines as well as usage criteria. We had a unique opportunity to capture a snapshot of their perceptions facing this complex ethical issue. We aimed to examine whether there was a leading policy theme or if gaps exist needing to be bridged in the light of national effective management of future emergency situations. Although in times of crises clear accepted guidelines are expected, we investigated to reveal how personal characteristics such as age, gender, specific profession, and knowledge or previous experience influence the professional attitude regarding the ECMO allocation. This approach stems from insight of emphasizing the autonomy and accountability of doctors and other therapists, struggling to save lives alongside the perception to maximize benefit to society. The survey was conducted during a period when the shortage of ECMO machines for COVID-19 patients was a central topic in public discourse. The Israeli Ministry of Health also emphasized this issue within healthcare organizations and held related training sessions to address it. The survey took place in January–February 2022, during the fifth wave of the Covid-19 pandemic in Israel. During a period when the scares resources for COVID-19 patients was a central topic in public discourse. participants apprised of the shortage of available devices (as shown in September 2021, when Israel had a peak of 53 patients in need of ECMO machines and only 82 devices available [ , ]. This shortage was perceived as a huge threat even though the devices were available in Israel at 1.14 per 100,000 inhabitants, as against only 0.55 in the U.S. (approximately 6,000 ECMO machines available) [ ]. The Israeli Ministry of Health also emphasized this issue within healthcare organizations and held related training sessions to address it. Nonetheless, before the survey, participants were given a lecture that provided them with background information about ECMO device utilization and success rates in treating Covid-19 patients who deteriorated to a state of respiratory failure. This shortage was perceived as a huge threat even though the devices were available in Israel at 1.14 per 100,000 inhabitants, as against only 0.55 in the U.S. (approximately 6,000 ECMO machines available) [ ]. The Israeli Ministry of Health also emphasized this issue within healthcare organizations and held related training sessions to address it. Nonetheless, before the survey, participants were given a lecture that provided them with background information about ECMO device utilization and success rates in treating Covid-19 patients who deteriorated to a state of respiratory failure. Survey instrument A structured questionnaire was produced on the basis of our previous experience [ ]. To increase response rates and align with the research objective, demographic data was limited to cultural background. This was assessed through a single self-declared question to reflect the cultural background, by the primary language spoken in their household. The other items revolved around a scenario in which the number of patients who need ECMO treatment secondary to Covid-19 deterioration exceeded the number of available devices. In the first question, participants were introduced to five theoretical patients and were asked to choose which one of them should be treated with an ECMO machine. They could also choose a sixth option: prioritizing no one. The following questions examined the justification for prioritizing specific age groups: young patients (aged 18–30) and senior patients (aged > 65). For each of the age groups, participants were asked to choose the most reasonable justification among several options. Next, they were asked to score their relative agreement with the decision to promote six different patients in queue for ECMO treatment in the case of a shortage of machines. The permissible answers ranged from ‘1’ (Definitely do not promote) to ‘4’ (Definitely promote). The 1–4 response scale was selected specifically to avoid central choices bias among hesitating respondents and more accurately reflect their true preferences. Finally, the participants were asked to score their relative agreement with the decision to promote six different theoretical patients in queue for ECMO treatment in the case of a shortage of machines, including a patient that refused to be vaccinated even though was able to do so. The allowable answers ranged from ‘1’ (opposed to postponing treatment) to ‘10’ (highly supportive of postponing treatment). See ‘Additional file 1’ for the exact wording. The participants were briefed on the importance of ECMO machines and their necessity as a lifesaving technology in the context of COVID-19 pandemic. Moreover, the shortage of these machines poses a dilemma regarding their allocation. To avoid biased decisions, no additional details were provided to the participants regarding unique features of each case. To summarize, our methodology integrated two independent prioritization concepts: the first, is prioritization actually required, and if so, what is the “correct” manner (order). The second- focus on the appropriate justification for each patient chosen, regardless of prioritization criteria. Analysis Differences between the Jewish and the Arab subgroups were calculated using X 2 tests for the nominal variables, as this test is suitable for assessing differences in categorical distributions between independent groups (the item relating to the choice of a particular patient and the items concerning the choice of the most appropriate justification for prioritizing the young and senior age groups). t -tests were used for the scale-based variable (the items relating to promoting and demoting), which were treated as continuous and met the assumptions of normality and independence. All tests and the extraction of descriptive statistics from the sample were conducted using SPSS 25 (SPSS Statistics, IBM, Armonk, New York). Results Altogether 228 participants were approached and agreed to participate in the survey; 226 completed the survey questionnaire. Their demographic characteristics by subgroup are presented in Table . Among the 226 responders, 130 (58%) were Jewish. Both subgroups were predominantly represented by females and by those holding nursing positions. Mean age and years of experience were lower among Arab compared to Jewish participants (34.4 vs. 41.05 years and 9.27 vs. 14.19 years, respectively). First, we examined the participants’ willingness to prioritize one patient as eligible for an ECMO device treatment. Table shows the distribution of responses to the question of regarding the justification for ECMO allocation by each “theoretical patient” (case) in the scenario of treatment shortage. The participants could also declare none of the “theoretical patients” should be prioritized. Table ; Fig. presents the distribution of the respondents’ choices of a single theoretical patient out of five patients to be eligible for treatment on the one available ECMO machine. Among participants who declared choosing one specific patient for prioritization, Arab participants significantly tended to prefer an elder ( X 2 = 4.04, p <.05) as well as the youngest patient ( X 2 = 3.51, p <.05) compared to Jewish participants. Next, we delved into the options of choosing young and elderly patients further, examining the participants’ justifications for their choices. Table shows the distribution of the answers among the possible justifications. As can be seen, no differences were observed between Arab and Jewish participants regarding the justifications for prioritizing the young patient. However, when it came to prioritizing the elder, Jewish participants tended to highlight the fact that seniors ‘have paid for health insurance all their lives’ and thus deserve priority (21, 16% vs. 8, 9%; X 2 2 = 3.02, p <.05). Contrastingly, Arab participants tended to claim that prioritization for the elderly stems from respect to their wisdom and social dignity, based entirely on their cumulative life experience (14, 15% vs. 7, 5%; X 2 = 5.85, p <.05). Notably, both Jewish and Arab professionals highly (69%) and similarly justify prioritizing the elderly, secondary to their complex medical condition. In alignment with this, 90.5%−90.6% justified prioritizing younger adults due to their good chances of recovery. Finally, we examined our participants’ perspective on the possibility of promoting or demoting different patients in the queue for ECMO treatment irrespective of other candidates. Table , and Fig. presents the mean values (and standard deviations) of the extent of agreement to promote six different theoretical patients and delay treatment for a person who refused to get vaccinated for Covid-19 even though she/he could have done so. In all cases, the mean answers ranged across the medium levels (2–3 for items relating to promoting patients, 4–5 for the demotion item). Significant mean differences were observed regarding the deprived person and the vaccine refuser. Specifically, Arab participants tended more strongly, compared to Jews, to prioritize the deprived person (2.48 vs. 2.21, t = 2.29, p <.05), Jewish participants were more willing to deprioritize a person who refused to get vaccinated (5.22 vs. 4.06, t= −2.78, p <.01). Discussion Allocation of scarce life-saving technologies poses a complex ethical challenge to healthcare professionals and policymakers. Even as the Covid-19 pandemic forced professionals to cope with this task in real practice, many healthcare providers lacked appropriate mechanisms or guidelines to do so [ , , ]. In this study, we examined the perceptions of healthcare professionals at the early stages of their medical journey and compared the standpoints of Jewish and Arab participants in order to assess the impact of cultural elements on their points of view. We focused on junior healthcare professionals who were attending a management preparatory program considered as a critical junction in their career. We also believe that the acute ethical dilemma that we introduced – prioritizing patients in need of ECMO care – is a high-level professional quandary that maximizes their ability to present ethical-based medical reasoning as a guide to their medical thinking. During the Covid-19 pandemic, ECMO devices offered promise and constituted a significant game-changing tool. The uniqueness of this study is that our participants were surveyed in the midst of an actual threat, a time when the supply of ECMO devices for Covid-19 patients was truly insufficient [ ]. These circumstances gave us the opportunity to examine the professionals’ preferences in real time. Another interesting point was the ability to scrutinize responses by cultural background, given our conviction that cultural and personal experience may influence therapists’ decisions and actions beyond the bare clinical details. The findings revealed several similarities as well as differences between the two subpopulations. We examined the leading justifications for prioritizing patients by age (distinguishing the young (35 Years old) and seniors (65 years old), the second question). Interestingly we observed, on the one hand, a tendency to prioritize younger people because of their chances of survival and the elderly, secondary to their complex medical condition. These findings indicate the choices were based mainly on clinical considerations rather than values related to the patient’s age and reflect the utilitarian approach: an attempt to reach and maximize the (clinical) benefit, regardless social or cultural aspects of the age. Interestingly we observed, on the one hand, a tendency to prioritize younger people because of their chances of survival and the elderly, secondary to their complex medical condition. These findings indicate the choices were based mainly on clinical considerations rather than values related to the patient’s age and reflect the utilitarian approach: an attempt to reach and maximize the (clinical) benefit, regardless social or cultural aspects of the age. Simultaneously, we found equal measures between the subgroups in their preferences to less prioritize ECMO treatment to other theoretical patients, although they have contributed to the community, have dependents, and are poor people. On the other hand, Arab professionals were more likely than their Jewish colleagues, to choose only one particular patient out of several given options, thus declaring a focused preference regarding specific allocation of scares devices. Interestingly, cultural related opinions exposed different justifications and considerations: for example, senior-adults were differently acknowledged by Arab professionals, who justified their treatment prioritization based on respected to their age and experience, beyond their medical considerations. Arab professionals also tended, more than their Jewish peers, to promote deprived individuals in the queue for ECMO treatment and not to deprioritize a person who refused to get vaccinated for COVID-19 even though they could, showing tolerance to marginal individuals of the society. This finding may reflect broader value systems embedded within collectivist cultural orientations, where communal responsibilities and social cohesion play a more prominent role in shaping ethical decisions, particularly under conditions of resource scarcity. Analyzing the Arab professionals’ preference pattern reveals a unique culture-based social attitude and distinctive moral values that may conflict with Jewish professionals’ utilitarian approach, indicative of professionalism, emphasizing the clinical significance as the leading consideration in allocation. They may concern the ‘rule of rescue’, meaning the desire to help the patient who is currently suffering the most 3 – and the deep respect for older members of society as a fundamental value and social pillar in Israeli Arab culture [ – ]. Contrastingly, Jewish professionals justified prioritizing the elderly by noting that they had paid for health insurance all their lives, reflecting distributional justice and reciprocity for past contribution. Limitations of the study First, the survey was based on a convenient sample that was designed to harvest from various managerial education programs, resulting in a disproportionate representation of nurses compared to physicians. Given that perspectives, fundamental training, professional backgrounds, and skill sets may differ substantially between nurses and physicians, future studies should strive to achieve balanced representation across these subgroups. Second, the recruitment of participants was from all national geographic districts; however, we observed lower responsiveness in the Southern District. Third, we targeted junior medical managers that have reached a specific career junction; it is possible that therapists in different stages of professional experience would have yielded different perceptions. Fourth, the sample was heterogeneous across several demographic variables (e.g., profession, age), which may confound group-level comparisons. In particular, comparisons between Jewish and Arab participants should be interpreted with caution, as differences in demographic characteristics may have influenced responses independently of cultural or ethnic identity. Fifth, the hypothetical nature of the scenarios presented to participants may not fully reflect the emotional intensity and pressure experienced in real-life ECMO allocation decisions. While the survey was conducted during an actual wave of the pandemic, future studies could incorporate simulations or retrospective interviews to better capture the complexity of real-time decision-making processes. Finally, the questionnaire was written solitary in Hebrew. The decision not to provide translations was based on two reasons: first, to avoid cultural bias emerging from wording and meaning that may fade during translation; and second, because all medical professionals in Israel are required to have proficiency in Hebrew, as bed side professional discussion are conducted in Hebrew. We prioritized standardization over the potential risk of lower response rates among participants whose primary language is Arabic, which ultimately did not occur. Future studies may use additional representative sampling methods to examine the influence of culture on healthcare providers’ resource allocation preferences and test it alongside professional factors such as career stage and clinical specialty. Conclusions Our survey focused on the perspective of junior medical managers, evolving to be the future managers of the healthcare system. As such, they may have to repeatedly face allocation dilemmas in the circumstances of emergency and uncertainty, similar to that emerged by the Covid-19 pandemic. Our findings demonstrate range of values between cultures, meaning differences between Jewish and Arab participants within the partnership of healthcare provision. While addressing dilemmas of allocating scarce resources in such a diverse society, mutual efforts should be made to bridge cultural gaps towards a national strategy. As such, they may have to repeatedly face allocation dilemmas in the circumstances of emergency and uncertainty, similar to that emerged by the Covid-19 pandemic. Our findings demonstrate range of values between cultures, meaning differences between Jewish and Arab participants within the partnership of healthcare provision. While addressing dilemmas of allocating scarce resources in such a diverse society, mutual efforts should be made to bridge cultural gaps towards a national strategy. Several studies, particularly those that examine the multicultural environment of Jewish and Arab healthcare professional in Israel [ – ], point to the difficulty that healthcare professional belonging to minorities encounter in making their voices heard [ ]. Harmonizing all voices offers a better understanding of allocating dilemmas to increase the sense of bridging disparities. Critical consciousness may offer a possible response, raising a call for interaction with peers in order to apply empathetic imagination and humbly ‘promote authentic dialogue with colleges and recognize the value of everyone in the room’ [ ]. This approach could serve as a framework for identifying and addressing interpersonal differences through heightened awareness and education. Furthermore, it could be expanded to incorporate cultural competency training aimed at increasing awareness and mitigating potential implicit biases. Ideally, such training would become an integral component of standard educational programs for healthcare providers across all disciplines. Future studies could assess the effectiveness and impact of these interventions on professional behavior, decision-making processes, and patient care outcomes. The academic discourse concerning the allocation of scarce lifesaving technologies has not yet been discussed in close proximity to the concept of critical consciousness; we suggest that the lesson learned from this study may highlight the relationship between the two. It is already widely understood that ethical perceptions should be broadly embedded in clinical practice [ , ] and education [ ]. Professionals’ decision preference schemes regarding medical practice and perceptions of professionalism have already been found to be culturally dependent [ , , ]. This study reveals cultural gaps extend later in life, by professionals in the final stage of their managerial training. While the application of critical consciousness is highly recommended in light of today’s settings of healthcare work [ ], this practice may be scalable and transferable to any medico-ethical task that entails multicultural teamwork worldwide. In addition, the pedagogical theory behind critical consciousness may be expanded to other stages of professional training among students, interns, and even senior professionals. Early implementation in medical and nursing studies is recommended, providing the younger generation with tools for navigating ethical processes– tools that were clearly lacking among professional teams during the Covid-19 pandemic. Finally, we expect the entire healthcare leadership to commit to implementing this perspective, thus integrating a clinically measured socio-ethical understanding, specifically critical consciousness, into a wide range of stakeholders and values. We believe that critical consciousness offers an opportunity to increase ‘doing good’ and can affect the shaping of the next generation of educated, sensitive managers, committed to personal attention, empathy, cultural caring, and national values as well as other components of professionalism.
